statements.text: the danger of that snake oil is not only the mistakes that can be made, that is, the failings, and you all have identified some of those failings, but sometimes how they work all too well, the algorithms which are essentially, for most people in this world, black boxes, driving content to children.
statements.context: Senate hearing on AI risks and opportunities where Senator Blumenthal questions expert witnesses about algorithmic content targeting of children.

statements.text: All too often, black box algorithms—artificial intelligence (AI) and algorithms have become a blanket mechanism for denial, and the insurance companies insist that those AI mechanisms are proprietary. [...] But part of what needs to happen is to make them more transparent so that patients and providers know, along with the public, how they are being used.
statements.context: Opening statement by Senator Blumenthal as chairman of the Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations at a hearing on Medicare Advantage care denials and delays.

statements.text: I think everyone has agreed regulation is necessary, maybe through some kind of Federal agency, call it an administrative agency.
statements.context: Senate Judiciary Subcommittee on Intellectual Property hearing on AI, patents, innovation, and competition.

statements.text: I think the idea of a pause is totally impractical. So, let me ask any of you whether you think a pause on AI—I know it's a somewhat simplistic question, is a good idea and even doable?
statements.context: Senate Judiciary Subcommittee on Intellectual Property hearing on AI, patents, innovation, and competition.

statements.text: And open source software obviously can be an enormously important resource for innovation and invention, for science, standards, transparency. It can foster competition. At the same time, even in the near term, that kind of generative AI tool can be dangerously abused.
statements.context: Senate Judiciary IP Subcommittee hearing on AI, patents, innovation, and competition.

statements.text: There's a need for thought and consideration here before these models are just thrown into the wild, so to speak.
statements.context: Senate Judiciary Subcommittee on Intellectual Property hearing on AI, patents, innovation, and competition.

statements.text: And in a hearing that Senator Hawley and I had in a different Subcommittee of the Judiciary Committee, the Privacy and Tech Committee, we focused a lot on this idea of a new agency, licensing and registration, guardrails and safeguards, like, maybe what I call the nutrition label, means of distinguishing and stopping deep fakes, audio clones, and so forth.
statements.context: Senate Judiciary subcommittee hearing on AI, patents, innovation, and competition.

statements.text: Well, my takeaway from this panel is that we need to clarify Section 230 to say it doesn't apply to AI. Because if it does, we're in a whole new world of hurt.
statements.context: Spoken during a Senate hearing on Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights, summarizing a panel discussion.

statements.text: We're also working on legislation that would establish an oversight agency, some independent entity that would set common-sense rules, and a licensing regime for certain uses of AI, not to discourage any form of free expression either through that legislation or through any rewriting of Section 230. [...] Basic rules of the road can be a sustainable foundation on how we move ahead with AI.
statements.context: Senator Blumenthal speaks during a Senate hearing on Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights.

statements.text: I would like to think all the perils, of AI through an oversight entity that would license new models, would require testing and red teaming, require transparency, a notice when AI is used, but also accountability on the part of AI companies, and a means of enforcement.
statements.context: Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee hearing on governing AI through federal acquisition and procurement.

statements.text: This historic executive order is a massive step forward in our work to harness the incredible potential of AI, while also implementing safety standards to better protect American consumers and workers.
statements.context: White House fact sheet compiling reactions to President Biden's October 30, 2023 Executive Order on AI, featuring statements from Members of Congress.

statements.text: Thanks, Mr. Chairman. This week, as you all know, President Biden issued a pretty sweeping order on artificial intelligence (AI), and the issue of security is central to that order, covering issues like malicious deep fakes, cybersecurity of infrastructure, protections for AI models.
statements.context: Senate Armed Services Committee nominations hearing where Senator Blumenthal questions the National Cyber Director nominee on AI cybersecurity risks.

statements.text: We have developed a framework for legislation, including a licensing regime with an oversight entity and testing before products are released so as to prevent the kind of deep fakes and impersonations that so scare people.
statements.context: Senate hearing on AI philosophy and future impacts, with Senator Blumenthal outlining his subcommittee's legislative framework.

statements.text: It was literally my voice, content that could have easily been mistaken for something I said. [...] It sounded exactly like my voice.
statements.context: Senate hearing on AI-enabled scams, chaired by the Subcommittee on Consumer Protection, Product Safety, and Data Security.

statements.text: How would you compare, question for both of you, our capability in the artificial intelligence sphere as compared to the PRC?
statements.context: Senate Armed Services Committee hearing on the Department of Defense Authorization for Appropriations for Fiscal Year 2025.

statements.text: artificial intelligence [...] Senator Hirono. Secretary Austin, the Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Office, or CDAO, is responsible for accelerating the Department's adoption of data, analytics, and artificial intelligence. [...] Do you think the Department and CDAO are moving at the right pace to keep up with our adversaries who are capitalizing on applying information technologies in warfare? [...] Secretary Austin. The Department of Defense (DOD) is moving at a rapid pace to deliver artificial intelligence (AI) capabilities that meet the needs of our warfighters and the Department as a whole. We are doing this with a firm commitment to the responsible use of AI. [...] we are taking the necessary steps to test, evaluate, and manage these technologies to ensure that they are safe, secure, and effective.
statements.context: Written question for the record submitted by Senator Hirono to Secretary Austin in connection with the Senate Armed Services Committee's FY 2025 National Defense Authorization Act hearings.

statements.text: What is shared here is a right in one's own likeness and creation as a person, an individual right. And I think there ought to be a right to take legal action under that right. A right without a remedy is unavailing [...] But my question is really focused on watermarking. Maybe you can tell us—let me ask all the witnesses—how watermarking can complement rules requiring permission to use someone's likeness or voice or creation in a deepfake or impersonation or simply using it without permission.
statements.context: Senate Judiciary Committee hearing on the No Fakes Act, focused on protecting individuals from unauthorized digital replicas.

statements.text: And it's not about censorship, not about blocking communication. It's about a product that is overly sympathetic to the user and/or deliberately portrays itself as a licensed psychologist.
statements.context: Senate Judiciary Subcommittee hearing examining harms to children from AI chatbots, featuring questioning of witnesses by Senator Blumenthal.

statements.text: Can you commit that none of the airlines that are Members of Airlines for America use AI in that way?
statements.context: Senate hearing on airline competition where Senator Blumenthal questions an industry witness about discriminatory AI pricing.
